stem:
A 61-year-old man is referred by his GP after several months of episodic purple-red facial flushing and watery diarrhoea; on two occasions he has also become wheezy. Abdominal imaging shows multiple liver deposits, and urinary 5-HIAA is raised.

Where is the primary tumour most likely to be?
why_correct: Flushing, diarrhoea and bronchospasm with raised 5-HIAA indicate carcinoid syndrome. The commonest source is a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour of the small bowel, usually the ileum. Serotonin and other amines from gut tumours are normally inactivated by the liver, so the syndrome usually appears once liver metastases release mediators directly into the systemic circulation. Source: Cancer Research UK, Carcinoid syndrome (neuroendocrine tumours), 2025.
why_wrong: A. An adrenal medullary tumour (phaeochromocytoma) causes paroxysmal hypertension, headache and sweating. B. Hepatocellular carcinoma is a primary liver tumour and does not produce carcinoid syndrome; the liver lesions here are metastases. C. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma causes weight loss, pain and painless jaundice. E. Sigmoid adenocarcinoma presents with change in bowel habit and rectal bleeding.
pearl: Right-sided heart valve disease (tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis) is a late feature of carcinoid syndrome.
thinking: Flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze ↓ Raised urinary 5-HIAA ↓ Carcinoid syndrome ↓ Liver metastases allow mediators into systemic circulation ↓ Primary usually small-bowel neuroendocrine tumour
exam_trap: B, Parenchyma of the liver — the liver lesions are obvious on imaging, but they are metastases that unmask the syndrome, not the primary source.
takeaway: Carcinoid syndrome usually arises from a small-bowel neuroendocrine tumour with liver metastases.

stem:
A 67-year-old woman on the medical admissions unit has vomited coffee-ground material twice and has had a black stool overnight. She has been resuscitated and is now stable.

Which investigation should be arranged to locate the source and allow treatment?

options.A: Lower bowel examination with a flexible sigmoidoscope
options.D: Ultrasound of the abdomen with Doppler

why_correct: Coffee-ground vomiting and melaena indicate an upper GI bleed. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy shows the bleeding lesion directly and allows treatment in the same procedure, for example clips, thermal coagulation, or adrenaline injection combined with a second method (adrenaline alone is not recommended). NICE advises endoscopy immediately after resuscitation for unstable patients and within 24 hours of admission for everyone else. Source: NICE CG141 Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s, 2012 (updated 2016).
why_wrong: A. Flexible sigmoidoscopy views only the distal colon. C. Colonoscopy cannot reach a source in the oesophagus, stomach or duodenum. D. Ultrasound cannot see mucosal lesions or stop bleeding. E. A barium meal cannot treat the bleeding point, and the contrast obscures the view at later endoscopy.
pearl: The Glasgow-Blatchford score is used at first assessment of upper GI bleeding, and the full Rockall score after endoscopy.
thinking: Coffee-ground vomit and melaena ↓ Upper GI bleed ↓ Resuscitate first ↓ Need to identify and treat the lesion ↓ Upper GI endoscopy
exam_trap: C, Full colonoscopy after bowel preparation — it is the standard test for rectal bleeding, but melaena here comes from an upper source beyond its reach.
takeaway: Upper GI endoscopy both diagnoses and treats the source of an upper GI bleed.
notes: Reviewer fix: Made NICE CG141 endoscopy timing precise: immediately after resuscitation if unstable, within 24 hours for others

stem:
A 53-year-old woman with primary biliary cholangitis and portal hypertension is admitted with haematemesis. After resuscitation and drug therapy, an urgent endoscopy shows actively bleeding varices in the lower oesophagus.

Which endoscopic procedure is preferred to control the bleeding?
correct_answer: B. Band ligation of the varices
why_correct: Endoscopic band ligation is the recommended treatment for bleeding oesophageal varices. Elastic bands placed around the varices strangulate them so that they thrombose and slough. If banding does not control the bleeding, a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) should be considered, with balloon tamponade as a temporary bridge. Source: NICE CG141 Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s, 2012 (updated 2016).
why_wrong: A. ERCP sphincterotomy treats bile duct stones, not varices. C. Cyanoacrylate injection is the endoscopic treatment for bleeding gastric varices; oesophageal varices are banded. D. Snare polypectomy removes colonic or gastric polyps. E. Argon plasma coagulation treats superficial lesions such as angiodysplasia, not variceal bleeding.
pearl: Everyone with suspected variceal bleeding should also receive terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation, before endoscopy.
thinking: Haematemesis in portal hypertension ↓ Endoscopy shows bleeding oesophageal varices ↓ Needs endoscopic haemostasis ↓ Bands strangulate the varices ↓ Band ligation
exam_trap: C, Injection of cyanoacrylate glue — it is a genuine endoscopic variceal therapy, but it is used for gastric varices; bleeding oesophageal varices are banded.
takeaway: Bleeding oesophageal varices are treated endoscopically with band ligation.

stem:
A 57-year-old female teacher sees her GP with several months of a dry cough that is worse at night and on lying flat, a hoarse voice by the end of the day and frequent throat clearing. Her chest examination and chest X-ray are normal and she does not smoke. On direct questioning she admits to a sour taste in her mouth and burning behind the sternum after large meals.

Which condition is most likely to explain her respiratory and laryngeal symptoms?
why_correct: Gastro-oesophageal reflux can cause extra-oesophageal symptoms such as chronic cough, hoarseness, throat clearing and a feeling of a lump in the throat, through acid irritation of the larynx and reflex vagal mechanisms. Her nocturnal, postural cough together with heartburn and acid brash points to reflux as the unifying cause. Because she has typical heartburn, a trial of acid suppression is reasonable; it is not advised for chronic cough without such evidence of reflux. Source: British Thoracic Society clinical statement on chronic cough in adults, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Achalasia presents with progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids and regurgitation of undigested food, not heartburn after meals. B. Eosinophilic oesophagitis typically causes dysphagia and food bolus impaction, often in young atopic men. C. Diffuse oesophageal spasm causes episodic chest pain and intermittent dysphagia rather than cough and hoarseness. D. Oesophageal candidiasis causes painful swallowing, usually in immunosuppressed people or inhaled steroid users.
pearl: Reflux is one of the commonest causes of chronic cough in non-smokers with a normal chest X-ray, alongside asthma and upper airway cough syndrome.
thinking: Chronic cough and hoarseness in a non-smoker ↓ Normal chest examination and X-ray ↓ Worse lying flat and at night ↓ Heartburn and acid taste after meals ↓ Extra-oesophageal manifestation of reflux disease
exam_trap: A, Achalasia of the cardia — it can also cause nocturnal cough from regurgitation and aspiration, but the leading symptom would be dysphagia to both solids and liquids, which she does not have.
takeaway: Chronic cough, hoarseness and throat clearing in someone with heartburn should prompt consideration of reflux disease.

stem:
A 52-year-old man of Irish descent has fatigue, aching in the knuckles of his index and middle fingers, and erectile dysfunction. His skin looks bronzed even in winter. Transferrin saturation and ferritin are both markedly raised and genetic testing confirms homozygosity for the C282Y mutation.

Which organ is the principal site of iron accumulation and of the most serious long-term complications?
why_correct: In hereditary haemochromatosis, excess absorbed iron is deposited mainly in hepatocytes. This causes hepatomegaly, fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis, which carries a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. The liver is therefore the main organ affected and the main driver of mortality, although the pancreas, heart, joints, skin and pituitary are also involved. Source: British Society for Haematology guideline on diagnosis and therapy of genetic haemochromatosis, 2018.
why_wrong: A. The kidneys are not a characteristic site of iron loading in haemochromatosis. B. The lungs are not a typical target organ. D. In hereditary haemochromatosis iron loads parenchymal cells such as hepatocytes; the spleen is relatively spared compared with transfusional overload. E. The thyroid can occasionally be affected but is not the principal organ.
pearl: Venesection is the mainstay of treatment, and when it is started before cirrhosis develops, survival is close to normal.
thinking: Fatigue, arthropathy of the second and third MCP joints and bronzed skin ↓ Raised transferrin saturation and ferritin ↓ C282Y homozygote confirms hereditary haemochromatosis ↓ Iron deposits mainly in hepatocytes ↓ Liver fibrosis, cirrhosis and liver cancer
exam_trap: D, Spleen — iron overload from repeated transfusion loads macrophages in the spleen, but in hereditary haemochromatosis it is the parenchymal cells of the liver that bear the brunt.
takeaway: In hereditary haemochromatosis the liver is the main site of iron deposition, leading to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

stem:
A 23-year-old woman with no history of liver disease is admitted after five days of vomiting and worsening yellowing of her skin. Over the last day her family say she has become muddled and drowsy. Her INR is markedly prolonged and she has a coarse flapping tremor.

What should be suspected?
why_correct: Acute liver failure is the rapid onset of jaundice, coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy in a person without pre-existing chronic liver disease. Her confusion and asterixis show encephalopathy, and the prolonged INR shows loss of synthetic function. She needs urgent discussion with a specialist liver unit, and causes such as paracetamol overdose and viral hepatitis should be sought. Source: Royal College of Emergency Medicine, RCEMLearning reference: Acute liver failure, 2024.
why_wrong: A. There is no history of alcohol misuse or chronic liver disease, so decompensated cirrhosis does not fit. B. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated jaundice without coagulopathy or confusion. C. Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia and eye signs, not jaundice and a raised INR. E. Gallstone obstruction causes cholestatic jaundice, but not encephalopathy and coagulopathy in this time frame.
pearl: Paracetamol overdose is the commonest cause of acute liver failure in the UK; the INR (prothrombin time) is a key marker of severity and prognosis and should not be corrected routinely, as it guides transplant decisions.
thinking: Previously healthy liver ↓ Rapid-onset jaundice ↓ Prolonged INR shows synthetic failure ↓ Confusion and asterixis show encephalopathy ↓ Acute liver failure
exam_trap: A, Decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis — jaundice, coagulopathy and encephalopathy also occur here, but by definition acute liver failure arises without pre-existing chronic liver disease, and nothing suggests cirrhosis.
takeaway: Jaundice, coagulopathy and encephalopathy in a previously healthy liver means acute liver failure.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl reworded: INR described as a key marker of severity/prognosis (not 'most sensitive marker') and note not to correct it routinely.

stem:
A 66-year-old man is seen in the surgical assessment unit with three days of yellow skin and a vague ache under the right ribs. He is afebrile. An abdominal ultrasound reports a common bile duct that is wider than normal, with dilated ducts inside the liver as well.

What is the most likely mechanism of his jaundice?

options.D: Blockage of the bile duct outside the liver

correct_answer: D. Blockage of the bile duct outside the liver
why_correct: Dilatation of the common bile duct and the intrahepatic ducts on ultrasound shows that bile is backing up behind a blockage in the extrahepatic biliary tree. In this setting the commonest causes are a stone in the common bile duct or a tumour of the pancreatic head or bile duct. Further imaging, such as MRCP, pancreatic-protocol CT or endoscopic ultrasound, then identifies the cause. Source: NICE CG188 Gallstone disease, 2014; NICE NG85 Pancreatic cancer in adults, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis causes unconjugated jaundice with normal-calibre bile ducts. B. Viral hepatitis is intrahepatic and does not dilate the bile ducts. C. Reduced bilirubin uptake, as with some drugs, gives unconjugated jaundice with normal ducts. E. Pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhoea and weight loss, not duct dilatation.
pearl: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging test in jaundice because duct dilatation quickly separates obstructive from non-obstructive causes.
thinking: Jaundice with right upper quadrant ache ↓ Ultrasound shows dilated common bile duct ↓ Intrahepatic ducts also dilated ↓ Bile is backing up behind a blockage ↓ Extrahepatic biliary obstruction
exam_trap: B, Hepatocellular inflammation from viral infection — hepatitis is a common cause of jaundice with right upper quadrant discomfort, but it does not dilate the bile ducts.
takeaway: Jaundice with dilated bile ducts on ultrasound means extrahepatic biliary obstruction.

stem:
A 35-year-old man with Crohn's disease is seen in the gastroenterology clinic during a flare of diarrhoea and abdominal pain. He also reports that his right ankle and left knee have become warm and swollen over the past fortnight. There is no history of injury and he has no rash or recent sore throat.

What is the most likely cause of his joint symptoms?
why_correct: Peripheral arthritis is the most common extra-intestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease. The type that involves a few large lower-limb joints typically flares with active bowel disease and settles as the bowel inflammation is controlled. Asymmetrical swelling of the knee and ankle during a Crohn's flare fits enteropathic arthritis. Source: British Society of Gastroenterology consensus guidelines on the management of inflammatory bowel disease in adults, 2019.
why_wrong: B. Gout typically presents as an acute monoarthritis, often of the first toe joint, and is not linked to bowel flares. C. Osteoarthritis is degenerative and does not cause warm, swollen joints in a young man in step with bowel activity. D. Post-streptococcal arthritis requires a preceding streptococcal throat infection, which he has not had. E. Haemarthrosis follows trauma or occurs with bleeding disorders or anticoagulation.
pearl: Large-joint pauciarticular IBD arthritis follows bowel activity, whereas axial disease such as sacroiliitis runs a course independent of the bowel.
thinking: Known Crohn's disease ↓ Currently flaring ↓ Warm swollen knee and ankle ↓ No trauma, rash or throat infection ↓ Enteropathic arthritis
exam_trap: B, Gout — an acutely warm swollen joint makes crystal arthritis tempting, but two large joints flaring with active Crohn's disease fit an IBD-related arthritis better.
takeaway: Inflammatory arthritis of large lower-limb joints during an IBD flare is enteropathic arthritis.

stem:
On a surgical admissions unit, a nurse documents that a 52-year-old woman has just had a large bowel motion consisting mostly of fresh, bright red blood. The team want the correct term for this finding in the notes.

Which term should be used?
why_correct: Haematochezia means the passage of fresh, bright red or maroon blood per rectum. It usually indicates a lower gastrointestinal source, although a brisk upper gastrointestinal bleed can occasionally present this way, with haemodynamic instability. Using the correct term helps colleagues triage the likely source quickly. Source: British Society of Gastroenterology guideline on acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Melaena is black, tarry, offensive stool from digested blood, usually from an upper source. B. Tenesmus is the feeling of incomplete evacuation with straining, not blood loss. C. Haematemesis is vomiting of blood. D. Occult bleeding is blood loss that cannot be seen and is found only by testing, such as a faecal immunochemical test.
pearl: Bright red rectal bleeding with shock should prompt consideration of a brisk upper gastrointestinal bleed, so upper endoscopy may be needed even when the blood looks fresh.
thinking: Fresh red blood passed per rectum ↓ Not black or tarry, so not melaena ↓ Not vomited, so not haematemesis ↓ Term for fresh rectal blood ↓ Haematochezia
exam_trap: A, Melaena — both describe blood passed per rectum, but melaena refers specifically to black, tarry stool from digested blood rather than fresh red blood.
takeaway: Haematochezia is fresh red blood per rectum; melaena is black, tarry stool.

stem:
A 45-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis tells his GP that his stools are pale, bulky, greasy and hard to flush. He has lost weight and bruises easily.

Deficiency of which group of nutrients is most expected?

options.C: Vitamins A, D, E and K

correct_answer: C. Vitamins A, D, E and K
why_correct: Pale, greasy, foul stools that are difficult to flush describe steatorrhoea, here from exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. The fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are absorbed with dietary fat, so impaired fat digestion leads to their deficiency. Easy bruising fits vitamin K deficiency causing a prolonged prothrombin time. Source: Pancreatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland, UK practical guidelines for the management of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, BMJ Open Gastroenterology, 2021.
why_wrong: A. Water-soluble B vitamins are absorbed independently of fat and are not the typical consequence of steatorrhoea. B. B12 absorption can be reduced in pancreatic insufficiency, but it is not the defining deficiency of fat malabsorption and does not explain the bruising. D. Vitamin C is water-soluble and is lost through poor diet, not fat malabsorption. E. Iron and folate are absorbed in the proximal small bowel and are more typical of coeliac disease.
pearl: In exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals is the mainstay, with supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins as needed.
thinking: Chronic pancreatitis ↓ Pale, greasy, hard-to-flush stools = steatorrhoea ↓ Dietary fat not absorbed ↓ Vitamins carried with fat are lost ↓ Deficiency of A, D, E and K (bruising from low K)
exam_trap: E, Iron and folate — these are common malabsorption deficiencies, but they reflect proximal small-bowel mucosal disease such as coeliac disease rather than failure to absorb fat.
takeaway: Steatorrhoea leads to deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

stem:
A 74-year-old woman who lives alone is admitted with a chest infection. Her neighbour says that since her husband died she has eaten almost nothing for about two weeks. She is very thin with marked muscle wasting, and her potassium and phosphate are at the low end of normal. The ward dietitian is planning to start nutrition support.

Which approach to feeding is most appropriate?

options.A: Give her full estimated energy requirements from day one to reverse weight loss quickly
options.B: Keep her nil by mouth for three days to allow the gut to recover
options.C: Start at a low energy intake with thiamine, monitoring and replacing electrolytes
options.D: Check electrolytes only after a week of full feeding
options.E: Give subcutaneous insulin with each feed to improve uptake of nutrients

correct_answer: C. Start at a low energy intake with thiamine, monitoring and replacing electrolytes
why_correct: About two weeks of negligible intake with marked wasting puts her at high risk of refeeding syndrome. In this syndrome, carbohydrate triggers insulin release and a rapid shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, with fluid retention and possible arrhythmias or heart failure. NICE advises starting nutrition at a low energy level and increasing it slowly over the first week. Thiamine and vitamin B supplements should be given immediately before and during the first days of feeding, and potassium, phosphate and magnesium supplemented and monitored closely. Source: NICE CG32 Nutrition support for adults, 2006 (updated 2017).
why_wrong: A. Full feeding from the start is exactly what precipitates refeeding syndrome in a starved patient. B. Withholding nutrition worsens starvation and has no benefit. D. Electrolytes fall within the first few days, so monitoring must start immediately. E. Insulin is not part of nutritional rehabilitation and would drive phosphate and potassium further into cells.
pearl: Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark biochemical abnormality of refeeding syndrome, typically appearing within the first two to four days of feeding.
thinking: About two weeks of negligible intake with marked wasting ↓ High risk of refeeding syndrome ↓ Feeding drives insulin release and intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium ↓ Start low and increase slowly ↓ Give thiamine and monitor and replace electrolytes
exam_trap: A, Full energy requirements from day one — rapid weight restoration seems like the goal, but in a starved patient it provokes dangerous falls in phosphate, potassium and magnesium.
takeaway: In severe malnutrition, refeed slowly with thiamine and close electrolyte monitoring and replacement.
notes: Checker: vignette changed from anorexia nervosa to an older adult with two weeks of negligible intake, because RCPsych MEED (2022) advises higher starting energy in anorexia nervosa; NICE CG32 applies directly to this patient.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman who takes ferrous sulfate for iron-deficiency anaemia phones NHS 111. For the past day her stools have been jet black, sticky like tar and unusually foul-smelling, and she nearly fainted when she stood up from her chair. Since starting iron her stools have been dark but formed, with no unusual smell.

What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Normal dark stools caused by oral iron

why_correct: Oral iron darkens the stool, but it does not make it tarry, sticky and offensive, and it does not cause postural near-syncope. That change in character, together with symptoms of volume loss, indicates melaena from an upper gastrointestinal bleed, and she needs emergency assessment in hospital. Her known iron deficiency may itself reflect an occult upper gastrointestinal lesion. Source: NICE CG141 Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s, 2012 (updated 2016); BNF, ferrous sulfate.
why_wrong: A. Iron makes stools dark grey-green or black but formed and not tarry or foul, and it never causes postural collapse. C. Diverticular bleeding usually presents with red or maroon blood rather than tarry stool. D. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause bleeding or haemodynamic symptoms. E. Haemorrhoids cause bright red blood on the paper or in the pan.
pearl: Melaena usually requires bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz with enough transit time for blood to be digested by gut enzymes and bacteria.
thinking: On oral iron, so dark stools are expected ↓ New change to tarry, sticky, offensive stool ↓ Postural near-syncope suggests significant blood loss ↓ This is melaena, not an iron effect ↓ Upper gastrointestinal bleed needing emergency assessment
exam_trap: A, Normal dark stools caused by oral iron — her iron therapy offers a reassuring explanation, but iron stools are not tarry or offensive and do not cause near-fainting.
takeaway: Tarry, offensive stool with postural symptoms is melaena from an upper gastrointestinal bleed, even in a patient taking iron.

stem:
A 34-year-old man who had extensive small-bowel resection for Crohn's disease is reviewed in the nutrition clinic. He has lost weight and says he can no longer find his way around his house at night and struggles to see when driving at dusk. His eyes look dry and wrinkled on the conjunctival surface.

Which deficiency is most likely?
why_correct: Vitamin A (retinol) is needed to form rhodopsin in the retinal rods, so deficiency first causes impaired vision in dim light. It also causes conjunctival and corneal dryness (xerophthalmia). As a fat-soluble vitamin, it is lost with fat malabsorption after small-bowel resection. Source: NHS website, Vitamins and minerals: vitamin A, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding and bruising, not night blindness. B. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with gum bleeding and perifollicular haemorrhages. C. Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia, bone pain and proximal weakness. E. B12 deficiency causes anaemia and neuropathy, and optic neuropathy is rare and not selective for dim light.
pearl: Vitamin A deficiency is a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide, and Bitot spots on the conjunctiva are a characteristic sign.
thinking: Malabsorption after small-bowel resection ↓ Fat-soluble vitamins at risk ↓ Poor vision in dim light = night blindness ↓ Dry conjunctiva = xerophthalmia ↓ Vitamin A deficiency
exam_trap: E, Vitamin B12 deficiency — terminal ileal resection does cause B12 deficiency, but it presents with anaemia and neuropathy rather than selective night blindness.
takeaway: Night blindness with dry eyes points to vitamin A deficiency.

stem:
A 49-year-old man with long-standing alcohol dependence is seen by his GP after his partner notices he has become forgetful and irritable. He has had loose stools for weeks, and the skin on his neck, face and the backs of his hands is red, scaly and darkened in a sharply demarcated pattern, worse after time outdoors.

Which deficiency is most likely?
why_correct: Pellagra results from deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3) and classically causes dermatitis in sun-exposed areas, diarrhoea and neuropsychiatric change, the so-called three Ds; untreated, it can be fatal. Alcohol dependence with a poor diet is a leading cause in the UK. The well-demarcated photosensitive rash around the neck is known as Casal necklace. Source: Patient.info Professional, Pellagra, 2023.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, not a photosensitive rash. C. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with gum disease, poor wound healing and perifollicular haemorrhages. D. B12 deficiency can cause cognitive change but not a photosensitive dermatitis or diarrhoea of this type. E. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain and muscle weakness.
pearl: Pellagra can also occur in carcinoid syndrome, because tryptophan is diverted to serotonin production, and with isoniazid therapy.
thinking: Poor diet with alcohol dependence ↓ Photosensitive, sharply demarcated dermatitis ↓ Chronic diarrhoea ↓ Cognitive and mood change ↓ Dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia = pellagra from niacin deficiency
exam_trap: D, Vitamin B12 deficiency — cognitive change in a malnourished drinker makes B12 tempting, but it does not explain a photosensitive rash with diarrhoea.
takeaway: Dermatitis in sun-exposed skin, diarrhoea and dementia point to niacin deficiency (pellagra).

stem:
A 61-year-old woman who lives alone and drinks heavily is assessed on a medical ward. Over several months she has developed burning feet, numbness in a stocking distribution and weakness climbing stairs. There is mild ankle oedema. She has been eating very little.

Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi: dry beriberi is a symmetrical sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy with muscle weakness, and wet beriberi adds high-output cardiac failure and oedema. Heavy drinkers with poor intake are at greatest risk. Thiamine should be replaced promptly, and parenterally if Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected. Source: NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications, 2010 (updated 2017).
why_wrong: A. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and dry eyes. B. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding gums and poor wound healing. C. Vitamin E deficiency can cause neuropathy and ataxia, but it is rare and usually linked to severe fat malabsorption rather than alcohol and poor diet. E. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding.
pearl: In anyone at risk of thiamine deficiency, give thiamine before glucose, because a glucose load can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
thinking: Heavy alcohol use and poor intake ↓ Symmetrical sensory neuropathy with burning feet ↓ Leg muscle weakness ↓ Ankle oedema hints at cardiac involvement ↓ Thiamine deficiency (beriberi)
exam_trap: C, Vitamin E — it can cause a neuropathy, which makes it tempting, but deficiency is rare and seen mainly with fat malabsorption, whereas alcohol and poor diet point to thiamine.
takeaway: Peripheral neuropathy and weakness in a malnourished heavy drinker suggest thiamine deficiency.
notes: Reviewer fix: thinking: 'Proximal weakness' changed to 'Leg muscle weakness' (beriberi weakness is not characteristically proximal)

stem:
On the hepatology ward, a 61-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and tense ascites has a steadily rising creatinine over a week, with very little urine output. Diuretics were stopped and he was given intravenous albumin, but his kidney function has not improved. He is not hypotensive and has not received any nephrotoxic drugs. Urine dipstick shows no blood or protein, and a renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Hepatorenal syndrome is a functional kidney injury in advanced liver disease caused by intense renal vasoconstriction. It is diagnosed when kidney function keeps deteriorating despite stopping diuretics and giving albumin, with no shock, no nephrotoxins, no proteinuria or haematuria and no structural abnormality on ultrasound, which matches this picture. Source: British Society of Gastroenterology and British Association for the Study of the Liver, guidelines on the management of ascites in cirrhosis, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis, which excludes obstruction. C. Glomerulonephritis would usually produce blood and protein on dipstick. D. Polycystic kidneys would be enlarged and cystic on ultrasound. E. Pyelonephritis would cause fever, loin pain and an abnormal urine dipstick.
pearl: First-line treatment of hepatorenal syndrome is terlipressin with albumin, but liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment.
thinking: Cirrhosis with ascites and rising creatinine ↓ Oliguria persists after stopping diuretics and giving albumin ↓ Bland urine and normal ultrasound ↓ No structural or intrinsic renal cause ↓ Functional renal failure of liver disease
exam_trap: A, Obstructive uropathy — oliguria with rising creatinine prompts thoughts of obstruction, but the ultrasound has already shown no hydronephrosis.
takeaway: Progressive kidney injury in cirrhosis that fails to respond to albumin, with bland urine and normal kidneys on scan, is hepatorenal syndrome.
